passage: Rehana, fifteen, lived above her father's cloth shop in Bijnor, and for months the headaches had kept coming back, a tight band behind her eyes. On the evening of her friend Lakshmi's mehendi, Rehana lay in the dark with a wet cloth on her forehead instead. "She's just moody," her Phuphi said from the doorway. "It's nothing. Girls her age make excuses." Rehana turned her face to the wall, hot with anger and shame. Lakshmi sent a voice note: "Missed you. Is it the headache again?" That night Abbu sat on the edge of the bed. "Nothing that keeps coming back is nothing. Tomorrow we go to the doctor in town." The doctor listened to every detail, wrote it all down and made a plan to find out more. On the bus home, Rehana's head still hurt a little, but she felt lighter. Someone believed her.

qa.q: What did Rehana lie with on her forehead?
qa.a: A wet cloth.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling when Phuphi called it nothing?
qa.a: She felt angry and ashamed, hurt at being dismissed when the pain was real.

qa.q: What made the biggest difference for Rehana, and why?
qa.a: Abbu taking her seriously and going to the doctor, who listened and planned to find out more; being believed lightened the emotional weight.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi seem to see Rehana missing the mehendi?
qa.a: Lakshmi misses her but understands, gently asking if it is the headache again instead of taking offence.

grounding: Shows a teenager with frequent headaches missing plans and feeling misunderstood when told it is nothing, then being taken seriously and properly checked.

passage: Freya had cancelled on Hiroshi three Saturdays running. Headaches, again. In their Glasgow kitchen her dad sighed, "It's all that screen time, love. You're just in a mood." Freya stomped upstairs, slammed her door, then cried into her pillow, which made her head pound harder. That night Hiroshi messaged: "You don't have to explain. Is your head really bad? Have you seen someone about it?" Freya read it twice. Nobody had asked like that. Next morning she told her mum how often it happened and how it made her feel like a liar. Her mum rang the doctor's surgery that day. At the appointment the GP asked careful questions, took notes and arranged some checks. "We'll work this out together," she said. Freya walked out still sore, but for the first time in weeks, not alone with it.

qa.q: Who rang the doctor's surgery?
qa.a: Freya's mum.

qa.q: How did Freya feel when her dad blamed screen time?
qa.a: She felt dismissed and angry, then upset enough to cry, because the pain was real.

qa.q: What helped Freya most, and why?
qa.a: Hiroshi's kind question, then telling her mum and seeing the GP; being taken seriously and checked properly eased the loneliness of the pain.

qa.q: How does Hiroshi respond to the cancelled Saturdays?
qa.a: Hiroshi does not take them personally, and instead asks with care whether Freya's head is bad and whether anyone has checked it.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager with recurring headaches cancelling plans and feeling dismissed, and relief when she is believed and properly checked.

subtype: Friend of someone in constant pain [Receiver]
passage: Ines had planned the beach day in Cascais for weeks. Early that morning Paulo texted: "Can't. Sorry." No explanation. Ines stared at the screen, stung. When she replied, "Again?", he wrote only, "Yes. Again." She spent the morning drafting angry messages and deleting them. By afternoon she took a tram to his Lisbon flat with a box of custard tarts. Paulo opened the door slowly, one hand pressed to his lower back, face grey. "Bad day," he said. Ines remembered what he had told her months ago: some days the pain took everything, even his words. "I'm not staying long," she said, handing him the box. "I just wanted you to know I'm not cross." His shoulders dropped. "Thanks. Next good day, the beach is on me."

qa.q: What did Ines bring to Paulo's flat?
qa.a: A box of custard tarts.

qa.a: She felt stung and angry, taking the curt "Yes. Again." personally.

qa.q: What choice kept the friendship kind, and why?
qa.a: Ines visited briefly with the tarts and said she was not cross, remembering that pain drains Paulo's energy and even his words.

qa.q: What was the cancelled day like for Paulo?
qa.a: It was a bad pain day that left him grey and short of words, and he seemed relieved that Ines was not cross.

grounding: Shows a friend of someone in constant pain hurt by a cancelled plan and curt replies, then choosing understanding over taking it personally.

subtype: Friend of someone in constant pain [Receiver]
passage: At the university library, Preeti had booked the group room for the four of them. Gurpreet arrived late, perched on the edge of her chair and snapped, "Can we just get this done?" when Preeti suggested going through the slides again. Preeti's cheeks burned. It was the third time this month Gurpreet had been curt or cancelled. Later, packing up, Preeti noticed Gurpreet standing to take notes, shifting her weight and wincing. She remembered Gurpreet saying in first year that her joint pain never really went away, only got louder some days. At the coffee counter Preeti asked quietly, "Is today a bad pain day?" Gurpreet nodded, eyes wet. "Sorry I bit your head off." "You don't have to be sorry. Next time, shall we meet in the ground-floor room with the softer chairs?"

passage:
Thursday
Back pain woke me before dawn again. I lay there counting what it has taken: the Munnar trek, Sunday cricket, the Bengaluru job I was meant to start this year. Some days it feels like mourning someone who's still alive, and that someone is me. Tonight I snapped at Harsha when she only asked if I wanted tea. I saw her face fall. Later I told her the truth: "It's not you. It's a bad day, and I'm sad about everything I thought I'd be doing." She held my hand and didn't try to fix it.
Things that help, so I remember: the physio's exercises, done slowly; resting before I crash, not after; the follow-up with Dr Mathew next week; saying it out loud instead of snapping.
Jomon

qa.q: What did Harsha ask before Jomon snapped?
qa.a: If Jomon wanted tea.

qa.q: What does Jomon feel about the plans the pain has taken?
qa.a: Jomon feels grief and sadness, like mourning a life that was planned.

qa.q: Which of Jomon's habits support both body and mood?
qa.a: Doing the physio's exercises slowly, resting before crashing, keeping the doctor's follow-up and being honest with Harsha instead of snapping.

qa.q: How was Harsha affected by the snap, and by the honest talk later?
qa.a: Her face fell at the snap over tea, but hearing the truth let her hold Jomon's hand instead of feeling pushed away.

grounding: Shows a young adult with long-lasting pain feeling irritable and grieving lost plans, and pacing, honesty and proper medical care supporting mood.

passage:
Counsellor's notes, joint session, pain clinic.
Sarika has lived with long-term pain for two years; her partner Nilesh came with her today. I watched how they spoke. When Sarika said mornings were the worst, Nilesh didn't argue or tell her to push through. He asked, "What would help today: the heat pad, quiet, or company?" When she answered sharply, "I don't know, stop asking," he said, "Okay, I'll check later," and his face stayed calm. Afterwards he told me privately that he used to hear her snaps as rejection and stay hurt for days. He now keeps his Saturday football and an early night midweek, "so I don't start keeping score". I told him both habits matter, and suggested they agree on a simple signal for bad days so Sarika needn't explain each time. We will meet again next month.

qa.q: What three options did Nilesh offer Sarika?
qa.a: The heat pad, quiet, or company.

qa.q: How did Nilesh used to feel about Sarika's snaps?
qa.a: He used to hear them as rejection and stayed hurt for days.

qa.q: What is wise about Nilesh keeping his Saturday football?
qa.a: Protecting his own rest and time stops caring from turning into resentment or keeping score.

qa.q: What might it mean to Sarika that Nilesh does not argue about her mornings?
qa.a: She feels believed rather than questioned, and can be honest about bad days without a fight.

grounding: Shows a partner of someone in pain asking what would help today, believing her, not taking sharpness as rejection and protecting his own rest.

passage:
Sunday night
Neelam's pain flared this morning, the kind that keeps her in the dark with the curtains shut. The old me would have hovered at the door, asking if she was sure she needed nothing, or worse, whether it was really that bad. Today I knocked once. "What would help today?" "Quiet. And warm water." I brought it and left. At lunch she snapped when I clattered a pan, and I felt the old sting, as if she didn't want me around. I reminded myself: that's the pain talking, not her. In the evening she came out, pale, and said sorry. I said there was nothing to forgive. Then I went for my walk by the lake, because when I skip my own rest, I start keeping score. Came back calmer and made dal. She ate a little.
Bhupen

qa.q: What did Neelam ask for?
qa.a: Quiet, and warm water.

qa.q: What did Bhupen feel when Neelam snapped over the pan?
qa.a: Bhupen felt the old sting of rejection, as if not wanted around, before remembering it was the pain talking.

qa.q: Why does Bhupen's evening walk matter?
qa.a: It protects Bhupen's own rest, so caring does not turn into keeping score and resentment.

qa.q: How might the day have felt for Neelam if Bhupen had hovered and questioned the pain?
qa.a: She would have felt doubted and crowded on a painful day, instead of believed and given the quiet she asked for.

grounding: Illustrates a partner asking what helps today, believing the pain without questioning, not reading irritability as rejection, and guarding their own rest.

passage: In their Pune flat, Eshaan, nearly two, would not let Zubin put him down. His cheeks were hot and his eyes glassy. He pushed his blocks away and wailed when a spoon fell. Zubin settled on the sofa with Eshaan on his chest, humming, and rang the clinic to ask what to watch for. He kept a close eye on him, just as the nurse described. "I've got you," he murmured, and Eshaan's fist loosened on his shirt.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan wail when a spoon fell?
qa.a: He felt ill and miserable, so even a small thing upset him and he wanted to be held.

qa.q: What might the afternoon have been like for Zubin?

grounding: Shows a feverish toddler wanting constant holding and crying at small things, with calm closeness alongside checking for warning signs.

passage: Swati, five, had given up her bottle months ago. But when the fever came, she dug the old sippy bottle out of the kitchen drawer in their Bengaluru flat and held it out to Sharmila. "Amma, milk in this. Pwease." Her visiting cousin giggled. "Baby talk!" Swati's lip wobbled. Sharmila filled the bottle, then turned to the cousin. "When we're poorly, we all want to be little again. It's okay." That night Swati slept curled in her parents' bed. Once the fever was gone, she announced the bottle was "for babies" and put it back in the drawer herself.

qa.a: In the kitchen drawer.

qa.a: The cousin might see it as comfort for a sick child rather than something to laugh at.

grounding: Shows a sick young child wanting a bottle, baby talk and the parents' bed again, and the regression fading as she recovers, without shaming.

passage:
"Mumma, can I sleep in your bed? Pleeease?" Jyoti's voice was small and croaky.
"You have your own bed, big girl," Papa said from the doorway.

subtype: Sibling annoyed by the sick child's attention [Receiver]
passage: All week in the Kolkata flat, everything was about little Mishti's fever: whispered phone calls, Ma sitting by her bed, soup on trays, cartoons on the big TV for Mishti only. Samir, nine, banged his school bag down and complained loudly that his homework was too hard. On Thursday he clutched his stomach at breakfast. "I think I'm sick too." His mother, Vasudha, felt his forehead, cool, and looked at his face. She didn't call it lying. "After school, you and I are going for a walk to the lake, just us. Mishti will be fine with Dadu." That evening Samir chattered the whole way round the lake, about cricket and the new boy in class. The stomach ache was never mentioned again.

qa.a: Busy and stretched, with her attention pulled to Mishti, yet she still noticed Samir needed her.

passage:
"Why does Tanu get dinner in bed on a tray?" Chandrika demanded.
"Because he's poorly," said Deepika, stirring the soup.
"I'm poorly too." Chandrika coughed loudly. "Very poorly."
Deepika looked at her daughter properly for the first time that day. "You've been missing me, haven't you?"
Chandrika shrugged, then muttered, "Everyone just asks about Tanu. Even Nani on the phone."
"That's hard. You've been so helpful this week, and I haven't said so." Deepika turned off the stove. "Tanu's asleep. Want to do our crossword on the balcony, just us two?"

passage: In their village near Satara, Samir lay under two blankets, aching, while the cricket tournament's loudspeaker crackled from the school ground. "I'm quitting the team," he croaked when Rajni brought rice kanji. "They'll drop me anyway. And I'm leaving tuition. What's the point?" He glared at the ceiling, then at her. "And stop checking on me!" Rajni set the bowl down. "You can decide all that. Just not today. Your head is full of fever. Big decisions can wait till you can stand without wobbling." "But the board exams, I'm missing classes..." "Sunita will bring notes. Today your only job is rest." She added quietly that if the fever kept going or worried them, they would take the bus to the doctor in town. The next week Samir was back on the ground, bowling badly and grinning. He never mentioned quitting.

passage:
Dear Yamini di,
You said to write when college got hard, so here it is. Last week I got a fever in the hostel. My roommate had gone home, and I lay alone in the dark, sweating and shivering, feeling about seven years old. I wanted Amma's rasam so badly I cried. I didn't tell anyone. I kept thinking: everyone's busy, I'm an adult, don't make a fuss. By the second night I couldn't get up to fill my bottle. That scared me. I finally messaged my friend Arvind down the corridor. He came with water and told the warden, and she took me to the campus clinic that morning. I'm better now. Next time I won't wait. I'll message someone straight away.
Love,
Sumit

qa.q: Who did Sumit finally message?
qa.a: Arvind, a friend down the corridor.

qa.q: Why didn't Sumit tell anyone at first?
qa.a: Sumit felt lonely and homesick but reluctant to bother anyone, thinking everyone was busy and an adult should not make a fuss.

qa.q: What will Sumit do differently, and why is it wiser?
qa.a: Message someone straight away next time, because reaching out early makes being ill safer and less lonely.

qa.q: How might Yamini feel reading this?
qa.a: She would probably feel worried for Sumit but relieved that Arvind and the warden helped, and glad Sumit wrote.

grounding: Shows a student sick alone in a hostel feeling homesick and reluctant to bother anyone, and learning that reaching out early is safer.

passage: Sudha, it's Kunal. You're moving into the hostel next week, so let me tell you about my first fever there. Second month, I woke up burning, every bone aching. My roommate was away. I lay there scrolling photos of Mumma's kitchen, so homesick it hurt more than the fever, and feeling very sorry for myself. I didn't text anyone. I thought they'd call me a baby. By evening I was dizzy walking to the bathroom. Then the warden, Mr D'Souza, knocked, because I'd missed dinner and he'd noticed. He took one look, called the doctor on duty and made me phone home. Mumma cried, then made me promise something. So here's the promise I'm passing on: if you're ill, tell your roommate, the warden or home that same day. Nobody will think you're a baby.

qa.q: Why did the warden knock?
qa.a: Kunal had missed dinner, and the warden noticed.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling alone in the room?
qa.a: Kunal felt deeply homesick and full of self-pity, and afraid of seeming like a baby.

qa.q: What advice does Kunal pass on, and why is it sound?
qa.a: To tell a roommate, the warden or home the same day when ill, because reaching out early makes recovery safer and less lonely.

qa.q: How did Mr D'Souza's noticing change things?
qa.a: He noticed the missed dinner, called the doctor on duty and got Kunal to phone home, turning a lonely night into getting help.

grounding: Illustrates a student ill alone in a hostel feeling homesick, full of self-pity and reluctant to bother anyone, and the case for reaching out early.

passage: Imran, it's Kashish. Before your first flu season here, let me tell you about mine. Last year I came into the office with a fever because I didn't want the team to think I was unreliable. New job, big client, you know. I sat there sweating, drinking tea after tea, and sent the client a report with last quarter's figures. Twice. Then I snapped at our manager when she asked if I was okay. By Friday, three people on our floor were ill, including an intern who had just started. So what did I actually prove? That I was reliable at spreading germs. This year, when I felt it coming on, I messaged the team: "Unwell, resting today, here's where my files are." Nobody minded. The work waited. That's the more responsible choice, honestly.

qa.q: What did Kashish send the client by mistake?
qa.a: A report with last quarter's figures, twice.

qa.q: Why did Kashish come in with a fever last year?
qa.a: Kashish was afraid of seeming unreliable in a new job with a big client.

qa.q: What did Kashish do differently this year, and why was it better?
qa.a: Kashish messaged the team, rested and shared where the files were, which protected colleagues and avoided mistakes.

qa.q: How were Kashish's colleagues affected by last year's choice?
qa.a: Three people on the floor fell ill, including a new intern, and the manager got snapped at for asking kindly.

grounding: Shows a young professional working with a fever out of fear of seeming unreliable, making mistakes and spreading illness, then choosing to rest and tell the team.

passage: I'm Lokesh, and I sit across from Sarika in accounts. On Monday she came in wrapped in a shawl, eyes watery, sneezing into tissue after tissue. When I asked, she said, "Just a cold. I can't miss audit week." By noon she had entered two invoices in the wrong month; I caught one of them. She kept saying sorry. I couldn't tell if she felt more ill or more scared. Our team lead, Farida, walked over, looked at her and said, "Home. Rest. Tell me what's urgent and I'll share it out." Sarika looked close to tears, relieved or embarrassed, I'm not sure. By Thursday two more of us were sniffling anyway. She came back the next week, much brighter, and caught a mistake of mine.

qa.q: What was Sarika wrapped in on Monday?
qa.a: A shawl.

qa.q: What might Sarika have been worried about by coming in?
qa.a: She was worried about missing audit week and letting the team down, perhaps scared of seeming unreliable.

qa.q: What did Farida's response get right?
qa.a: Sending Sarika home to rest and sharing out the urgent work, which protected both Sarika and the team from mistakes and illness.

qa.q: How does Lokesh see Sarika's choice to work?
qa.a: Lokesh notices the errors and the illness spreading, but cannot tell whether Sarika felt more ill or more scared.
